翌.meaning: A peacock refuses to practise its big tail display, so every night it hangs its <part>feathers</part> on a coat <part>stand</part> by the bed and promises to do it 'tomorrow'. Each morning the feathers are still on the stand, and the peacock just taps the calendar: it always means the <kanji>following</kanji> day.
翌.on: Instead it eats a runny egg <sound>yolk</sound> in bed and leaves the plate for tomorrow too.

卵.meaning: The sheriff kicks open the <part>saloon doors</part> and finds the bar empty except for a nervous hen on the piano. Behind each swinging half lies one small white <part>dot</part> she left as she fled the noise. The sheriff tips his hat and carries them out very gently: each one is an <kanji>egg</kanji>.
卵.on: He hands them to a pilot, who taxis them down the <sound>run</sound>way to a quieter town.
卵.kun: There the hen sells <sound>ta</sound>cos with a <sound>ma</sound>ma <sound>go</sound>pher, who keeps the eggs warm between orders.

帝.meaning: In the steamy sauna, one old man rules the top bench: a <part>towel</part> round his waist, a <part>blanket</part> over his shoulders like a cape, and a pot <part>lid</part> on his head with two <part>horns</part> glued on as a crown. Nobody dares pour water on the coals without his nod. He is the sauna's <kanji>sovereign</kanji>.
帝.on: His throne is an upturned bucket wrapped in silver <sound>ta</sound>pe.
帝.kun: A <sound>mee</sound>rkat fans him with a <sound>car</sound>p's tail while he nibbles a <sound>do</sound>lphin-shaped biscuit.

仰.meaning: At the post office, a clerk hangs his jacket on the <part>coat hook</part> and lies on the floor for his break, holding the <part>twin stamps</part> up above him. Every letter a colleague drops past his nose gets stamped twice from below. He spends the whole afternoon lying <kanji>face-up</kanji>.
仰.on: His lunch is a plate of <sound>gyo</sound>za, which he eats lying down, one by one.
仰.kun: '<sound>Ah</sound>,' he sighs, gazing up through the skylight at a sky full of <sound>o</sound>val clouds.

誠.meaning: A village has a magic well: any <part>speech</part> shouted into it comes back up, and every lie will <part>turn into</part> a frog that hops off croaking. A shy farmer whispers 'I love your bread' to the baker, and his words rise out as a single white dove. That's real <kanji>sincerity</kanji>.
誠.on: The baker locks one of the dove's feathers in her steel <sound>sa</sound>fe.
誠.kun: Her <sound>ma</sound>ma says he's as honest as a <sound>ko</sound>ala is sleepy, and carves the dove on the family <sound>to</sound>tem pole.

忠.meaning: Every night a lighthouse keeper's cat sits in the exact <part>middle</part> of the lamp room, its <part>heart</part> thumping each time the foghorn blares, yet it never leaves. Storms, seagulls, a tempting fishing boat: the cat stays at its post beside the keeper. That's <kanji>loyalty</kanji>.
忠.on: To pass the long nights, the two of them share a pack of <sound>chew</sound>ing gum and blow bubbles at the moon.

柱.meaning: A pompous <part>lord</part> brags that his new banquet hall rests on solid gold. During the feast the roof creaks, and the guests see that the only thing holding it up is one living <part>tree</part> growing through the floor, its branches spread under the ceiling. The lord hangs his crown on it and calls it his finest <kanji>pillar</kanji>.
柱.on: A squirrel on the trunk stuffs <sound>chew</sound>ing gum into every crack to keep it steady.
柱.kun: A <sound>ha</sound>rp plays, a <sound>shee</sound>p dances, and a bowl of <sound>ra</sound>men is set down at the tree's roots.

揚.meaning: A tiny fishing boat is stuck: its rusty <part>anchor</part> won't come up. The captain ties the chain to the morning <part>sunbeams</part>, and as the sun climbs, the anchor rises with it, dripping seaweed. She sips her tea and lets the sun do the work to <kanji>hoist</kanji> it.
揚.on: Once it's up, the anchor bobs on its chain like a giant <sound>yo</sound>-yo.
揚.kun: '<sound>Ah</sound>!' gasps the crew, as the anchor swings up past the mast.

慮.meaning: A <part>tiger</part> stops at a zebra crossing to <part>think</part>. He looks left, looks right, then left again, while the zebras on the stripes wait politely for him. Only when the green man shows does he stroll across, tail high. His mother taught him <kanji>prudence</kanji>.
慮.on: On the far side he orders one small glass of <sound>Rio</sound>ja and sips it very slowly.
慮.kun: Past the crossing he hums along to an <sound>o</sound>boe on the freshly <sound>mown</sound> verge, then shares <sound>pa</sound>sta with a <sound>coo</sound>k, pausing to ponder before every bite.

踊.meaning: Every night the museum locks its ballroom with a heavy <part>padlock</part>. At midnight a marble <part>foot</part> from the statue hall hops over, taps the lock open with its toes and twirls round the empty floor until dawn. The guard never wonders why the lock is warm. The foot loves to <kanji>dance</kanji>.
踊.on: It spins a <sound>yo</sound>-yo on its big toe as it waltzes.
踊.kun: An <sound>o</sound>boe plays from a dusty case, and a <sound>do</sound>lphin statue claps along.

絞.meaning: At the knitting club, two balls of <part>thread</part> <part>mingle</part> under the table, twist round each other and loop about the teapot. They pull tighter and tighter until the pot squeaks and tea squirts out of the spout. The knitters gasp: their yarn is trying to <kanji>strangle</kanji> the teapot.
絞.on: One knitter catches the squirting tea in an ice cream <sound>co</sound>ne.
絞.kun: Another squeezes the soggy wool out over a <sound>shee</sound>p-shaped cushion and a little <sound>bo</sound>nsai.

帳.meaning: A lifeguard has no paper, so he writes the name of every swimmer, every lost sandal and every jellyfish sighting on a very <part>long</part> beach <part>towel</part>. By August the towel trails down the sand, covered in ink. It's his <kanji>notebook</kanji>.
帳.on: When it's full, he starts scratching names onto his <sound>cho</sound>ker necklace.
帳.kun: At sunset he hangs the towel from a <sound>to</sound>tem pole as a curtain, so his <sound>bu</sound>dgie can sleep by the <sound>ree</sound>f.

垂.meaning: In a heatwave, a candle maker hangs his candles on a tall <part>pole</part>, <part>one</part> straight bar above another. By noon the top candle has bent into a soft <part>slash</part>, and the rest bow lower every hour, wicks pointing at the ground. All his candles <kanji>droop</kanji>.
垂.on: Below them, a child's <sound>swee</sound>t melts and bends over its stick.
垂.kun: In her other hand, a <sound>ta</sound>co flops over too.

嘆.meaning: A <part>husband</part> promises to mow the <part>grass</part> by the weekend. By Sunday it towers over the shed, and his wife finds him lying in it, staring at the mower. He opens his <part>mouth</part> and lets out one enormous <kanji>sigh</kanji> that flattens half the lawn by itself.
嘆.on: The kids turn the other half into a long grassy <sound>tun</sound>nel to crawl through.
嘆.kun: He sulks with a plate of <sound>na</sound>an while a <sound>ge</sound>cko sunbathes on the mower.

潔.meaning: A fussy spider tidies her web every morning. She cuts away each <part>snipped thread</part> a fly has broken, then rinses the whole web in dew, <part>water drops</part> shining on every strand. Not one speck of dust is left. Her web is <kanji>undefiled</kanji>.
潔.on: Then a picnic below squirts <sound>ketch</sound>up up at it, and she has to start again.
潔.kun: An <sound>ee</sound>l, a <sound>sa</sound>rdine and two <sound>gee</sound>se help her rinse it, then share a pot of <sound>yo</sound>gurt.

衰.meaning: A magician's glittering <part>garment</part> sheds sequins every night of his tour, until only <part>one</part> thin stripe of glitter is left across the middle. The rabbit retires, the doves fly off, and the last audience is three pigeons. His career is in <kanji>decline</kanji>.
衰.on: Fans used to throw roses; now one pigeon drops him a wrapped <sound>swee</sound>t.
衰.kun: His <sound>o</sound>boe player quits, his <sound>to</sound>tem pole prop cracks, and his <sound>ro</sound>dent assistant runs off with the hat.

誌.meaning: A parrot in the town hall repeats every <part>speech</part> it hears, along with each mayor's secret <part>intention</part> muttered under his breath. A clerk follows it around with a quill, writing it all down, stamping and dating each page. Every sheet is a <kanji>document</kanji> for the archive.
誌.on: She guards the archive door with a knight's <sound>shi</sound>eld.

猫.meaning: A gardener plants one tiny <part>seedling</part> and goes in for tea. Something with a claw curved like a <part>fishhook</part> digs it up, rolls in the soil and curls up in the hole for a nap, purring. The gardener sighs: his new flowerbed belongs to the <kanji>cat</kanji>.
猫.on: Later it wakes to swat a <sound>bee</sound> riding a <sound>yo</sound>-yo, up and down, all afternoon.
猫.kun: Then it stretches its <sound>ne</sound>ck and naps on a toy <sound>ko</sound>ala.

艦.meaning: In the bath, a rubber duck stands on the soap dish to <part>oversee</part> a little wooden <part>boat</part>. It fits it with a pencil cannon and a paper flag, salutes, and orders it to patrol the bubbles. The boy's bath toy is now a <kanji>warship</kanji>.
艦.on: Its first capture is a pink <sound>car</sound>nation floating by the taps.

城.meaning: A mole pushes up a pile of <part>soil</part> every night in the farmer's field. By the full moon the heaps <part>turn into</part> towers, walls and a drawbridge, and the mole moves in wearing a thimble crown. Now the farmer has to mow round his neighbour's <kanji>castle</kanji>.
城.on: A <sound>jo</sound>ey hops over the drawbridge for tea.
城.kun: A <sound>shee</sound>p and a sleepy <sound>ro</sound>dent stand guard at the gate.

巧.meaning: At his <part>workbench</part>, an old clockmaker can't reach his tiny tools, so he hooks each one with the crook of his <part>cane</part>, flips it into the air and catches it between two fingers. He builds a whole watch without standing up. His hands are <kanji>adroit</kanji>.
巧.on: For a break, he flips an ice cream <sound>co</sound>ne off the shelf and catches it too.
巧.kun: He even hooks a <sound>taco</sound> off his neighbour's plate without spilling a bean.

扇.meaning: In a stuffy café, the owner glues <part>feathers</part> all over the kitchen <part>door</part>. Every time a waiter barges through, it swings and whooshes a cool breeze over the customers, blowing their napkins away. The chef calls it the world's biggest <kanji>fan</kanji>.
扇.on: A <sound>sen</sound>try now stands by the door and swings it on cue whenever someone sweats.
扇.kun: '<sound>Ohh</sound>,' sighs a hot customer, as the next gust lifts two <sound>gee</sound>se off the pond outside.

童.meaning: The <part>farm</part>'s new scarecrow can't <part>stand</part> still. It giggles when crows land, sneaks apples from the barrels and swaps its hat with the goat's. One evening it climbs down and runs in for dinner. It was a mischievous <kanji>juvenile</kanji> in a straw hat all along.
童.on: In the kitchen he shapes a lump of bread <sound>dough</sound> into a crow.
童.kun: His mum hands him <sound>wa</sound>sabi peas and a bowl of <sound>ra</sound>men, then sends him to <sound>be</sound>d.

輝.meaning: An <part>army</part> marches out at dawn, but the general has made the soldiers polish their helmets so hard that the first <part>ray</part> of sun bounces off every one. The enemy is dazzled, squints, and goes home for sunglasses. The battle is won by pure <kanji>radiance</kanji>.
輝.on: The general's only medal is a polished brass <sound>key</sound>.
輝.kun: Back at camp the cook serves <sound>car</sound>p with <sound>gar</sound>lic, and the soldiers knit helmet covers from <sound>ya</sound>rn.

飼.meaning: A film <part>director</part> needs a wild raccoon for her movie. Each day she leaves a bowl of <part>food</part> a little closer to the set, until one morning the raccoon is sitting in her chair, wearing her cap and shouting 'Cut!' She meant to <kanji>domesticate</kanji> it, not hire it.
飼.on: Now it naps behind her desk on a knight's <sound>shi</sound>eld.
飼.kun: She also keeps a pond <sound>car</sound>p, which wants its own trailer.

湾.meaning: A <part>jellyfish</part> wants a quiet place to float, so it draws a <part>bow</part> and shoots an arrow at the coast. The cliffs bend inward like the curve of the bow, and the sea rushes in, <part>water drops</part> spraying. Now it has its own calm <kanji>gulf</kanji>.
湾.on: The fish say it <sound>won</sound> the prize for the prettiest coast.
湾.kun: An <sound>ee</sound>l moves into its <sound>ree</sound>f and lays an <sound>e</sound>gg there.

黙.meaning: A library hires a big <part>black</part> <part>dog</part> as its night guard. It never barks: when a burglar creeps in, it just stares from the dark shelves with two glowing eyes until he tiptoes out again. The librarian loves its perfect <kanji>silence</kanji>.
黙.on: It pads between the shelves in soft <sound>moc</sound>casin slippers.
黙.kun: Even the <sound>du</sound>ck in the pond and its <sound>ma</sound>ma stop quacking when it walks past.

煮.meaning: <part>Someone</part> on a camping trip has lost her kettle, so she fills her own rubber boot with water and sets it on the <part>hot coals</part>. Soon it bubbles, steams and smells faintly of socks. She makes tea anyway: water is water once you <kanji>boil</kanji> it.
煮.on: She fans the coals with a <sound>shu</sound>ttlecock to make it bubble faster.
煮.kun: Then she stirs the boot with a knitting <sound>nee</sound>dle.

祈.meaning: In thick fog, a lumberjack swings his <part>axe</part> at what he thinks is a tree. It's a <part>lamppost</part>, and the axe sticks fast. He tugs, then kneels under the glowing lamp, hands together, begging it to let go before the council finds out. All night, he can only <kanji>pray</kanji>.
祈.on: At dawn a cleaner opens a little door in the post with a <sound>key</sound>, and the axe drops out.
祈.kun: To say thanks, he leaves the lamp a smoked <sound>ee</sound>l and a handwritten <sound>no</sound>te.

盟.meaning: Two rival cooks, one who works by day and one by night, have to share one <part>dish</part> under a <part>bright</part> lamp in a tiny kitchen. The day cook bakes the base, the night cook adds the topping, and they sign a deal on the plate's rim in tomato sauce. The town's best pie comes from their <kanji>alliance</kanji>.
盟.on: They celebrate by getting lost together in a hedge <sound>ma</sound>ze.
